title: The stars streak overhead
caption: Star trails over the APEX telescope, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at APEX, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: It might look like abstract art, but this is a long-exposure photograph taken above the Chajnantor plateau, high in the Chilean Andes. As Earth turns, the stars of the Milky Way stretch into colourful streaks, and the telescope in the foreground takes on a dreamlike look.

The telescope is APEX, the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment, which stands 5000 metres above sea level. It is 12 metres across and collects millimetre and submillimetre light, which astronomers use to study everything from cold clouds of gas and dust where stars are born to some of the earliest, most distant galaxies.

APEX is a pathfinder for ALMA, built on the same plateau. The two complement each other: APEX's wider field of view lets it find many targets across large areas of sky, and ALMA's much sharper resolution lets it study them in detail. Both help astronomers learn how stars like those wheeling overhead come to form.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure landscape photograph; the source gives no specific camera settings.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as points; the long exposure records Earth's rotation, stretching them into coloured streaks.

explore: The photographer, ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi, also founded The World At Night, which pairs landmark sites with the night sky. APEX is run jointly by ESO, the Onsala Space Observatory and the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy.
alt: Colourful star streaks across the night sky above the APEX telescope on a high plateau.
